_doc: A line on each of the city's venues (see venues.json, built by scripts/build_map.py) — what anyone who knows Gotham knows of them. Read by the Codex and by places.note; his own edits in the Codex take precedence.

notes.Bleak House: A Dickens-themed pub in a listed Old Gotham townhouse: candles in bottles, a fire that never goes out, and lawyers from the courthouse pretending they aren't drinking at noon.
notes.Copper Kettle: A dockworkers' bar in Waterloo with copper-topped tables worn green; shift whistles are the only clock anyone trusts in here.
notes.Dock 9: A shipping-container bar on the Port's Park waterfront — cheap beer, a forklift for a doorman, and cargo nobody asks about in the back lot.
notes.Gin Alley: A Narrows gin joint down a passage you'd walk past twice; the bathtub gin is a joke on the menu and possibly not a joke.
notes.Kane's Tap: Burnside's craft-beer bar, eighteen taps and a chalkboard of pours named after Gotham's founding families, none of them flattering.
notes.Last Call: A Bowery dive that opens at four in the afternoon and shuts when the bartender cries. The jukebox has three working songs.
notes.O'Malley's: The Bowery's oldest Irish bar: cops at one end, the people they arrest at the other, and a truce about the dartboard.
notes.Saint Mike's: A Crime Alley bar in a deconsecrated chapel; the confession booth is a snug and the priest-collared barman hears plenty.
notes.Shamrock: A Tricorner shot-and-beer bar where the longshoremen's union still holds meetings, and the meetings still end in fights.
notes.The Corner Pocket: A Crime Alley pool hall with sticky felt and sharper players; half of Gotham's small-time debts get settled over the eight ball here.
notes.The Crooked Mile: Burnley's neighbourhood local, crooked floorboards and all — trivia on Tuesdays, and a regular who's won it since 1998.
notes.The Drowned Man: A Tricorner waterfront bar with a ship's figurehead over the door and a bell rung for every sailor who doesn't come back.
notes.The Hollow: A Narrows basement bar under a boarded-up laundromat; no sign, no windows, and the best whiskey in the worst part of town.
notes.The Iron Stool: An Old Gotham bar built from a foundry's leavings — stools welded to the floor after one too many were thrown.
notes.The Lantern: A Burnley bar strung with a hundred paper lanterns; quiet, warm, and where first dates go to see if there'll be a second.
notes.The Nightjar: A Waterloo cocktail bar that opens at midnight; Blüdhaven's night-shift nurses and cops drink side by side and say nothing.
notes.The Rusty Anchor: A Chinatown sailors' bar from when the docks came this far inland: nets on the ceiling, mahjong in the back, and a parrot that swears in Cantonese.
notes.The Wet Rat: A Robinsville dive whose flooded basement gave it the name and kept the health inspector away for a decade.
notes.Black Cat Café: Avalon Heights' cat café — eleven cats, one of whom has bitten a city councillor and is a local hero for it.
notes.Café Lune: A Halyard Square café with moon-phase pastries and a patio that catches Blüdhaven's one sunny hour.
notes.Common Grounds: Old Gotham's quiet coffee house, chess boards on every table and a no-phones rule the owner enforces with a stare.
notes.Cup of Joe's: A University District coffee counter open twenty-four hours for the thesis crowd; the refills are free and the despair is ambient.
notes.Drip: A Burnside pour-over bar where a cup takes eleven minutes and the baristas have opinions about your choices.
notes.Grindhouse Coffee: Upper West Side espresso in a former grindhouse cinema, horror posters still on the walls and slasher films on Fridays.
notes.Kettle & Crow: A Coventry tea-and-coffee house in a converted rookery, crows on the sign and real ones on the gutters.
notes.Moka: A Cherry Hills café where the old money takes its Sunday brunch and pretends not to see who's sitting with whom.
notes.Perk: A Diamond District grab-and-go for traders, open at five and out of everything by nine.
notes.Pour House: A Burnside coffee shop by day and open-mic bar by night; the poetry is mostly about Gotham and mostly bad.
notes.The Daily Grind: The University District's student café, where every table has a laptop and every laptop has a deadline.
notes.The Roastery: A Fashion District roaster that sources single-origin beans and sells them to models in very small cups.
notes.Third Wave: A Burnside café-bike shop hybrid — oat milk at the front, derailleurs at the back, both priced like art.
notes.Grace Chapel: A small Burnley chapel that runs the soup kitchen on Fridays and asks nobody's name at the door.
notes.Holy Trinity: Coventry's Episcopal church, red-brick and tidy, with a bell tower the kids dare each other to climb.
notes.Our Lady of the Harbor: The Tricorner fishermen's church; the nets are blessed every spring and the dead are remembered on a wall of names.
notes.St. Aidan's: Bristol's parish church, all flint and stained glass — the Waynes' pew is near the front and usually empty.
notes.St. Jude's: An Old Gotham church for lost causes, fittingly; the candle stand by the door never goes dark.
notes.St. Swithin's: A crumbling Old Gotham church whose roof leaks on the altar every time it rains — so, always.
notes.Cineplex 12: An Old Gotham multiplex with sticky floors and twelve screens, three of which have working sound.
notes.Majestic: Blüdhaven's grand old picture palace in Halyard Square, gilt and velvet, running classics to half-empty rows.
notes.Odeon Gotham: The Fashion District's premiere house — red carpets, flashbulbs, and Bruce Wayne leaving early through a side door.
notes.Starlite Drive-In: Burnside's drive-in on the old rail yard, double features under the stars and the bridge lights.
notes.The Bijou: A Kane Heights art-house cinema showing foreign films to people who'd rather you knew they'd seen them.
notes.The Paramount: A Diamond District movie palace restored with Wayne Foundation money; the organ still rises out of the floor before the feature.
notes.The Rex: A New Town cinema with recliners, cocktails and tickets priced to keep New Town new.
notes.Ace of Clubs: A Fashion District casino-club: card tables upstairs, a dance floor below, and a dress code enforced by very large men.
notes.Babylon: A Crime Alley megaclub in a former bank vault — bass you feel in your teeth and a VIP room behind a real safe door.
notes.Catacombs: A Bowery club in the old subway tunnels, candles in skull sconces and a crowd that dresses for the theme every night.
notes.Club Noir: A members-only CBD jazz club, black lacquer and smoke; deals get made in the booths that never make the papers.
notes.Grin: A Diamond District club everyone says the Joker once owned; the owner encourages the rumour and the smile on the sign.
notes.Low Tide: A Fashion District club at water level with glass floors over the river — models, money and the odd fish.
notes.Midnight Mass: A Crime Alley goth club in an old church: organ remixes, black lipstick and a strict no-daylight policy.
notes.Neon Saint: Burnside's queer dance club, pink neon halos and the best Saturday night in the city by a mile.
notes.Sixth Sin: A CBD club themed on the seven deadly sins — the sixth floor is envy, and the bouncers decide who gets in.
notes.Smoke & Mirrors: A Chinatown magic club where the tricks are real and so, some say, is the gambling in the basement.
notes.Static: An Amusement Mile electronic club in a dead arcade, pinball machines for seats and the Ferris wheel lit through the windows.
notes.The Aviary: An Old Gotham rooftop club among the gargoyles — the Penguin's crowd, some nights, and nobody admits it.
notes.The Blue Mask: A Crime Alley masquerade club; everyone's in a mask and nobody's who they say, which suits everyone.
notes.The Gilded Cage: An Old Gotham burlesque club in a birdcage-shaped room, the dancers in swings and the tips in gold.
notes.The Gutter: An Amusement Mile punk dive by the boardwalk, sticker-plastered and loud enough to drown out the roller coaster.
notes.The Laughing Fish: A Burnside comedy club named after the most infamous Joker stunt; the comics do the bit, the city winces.
notes.The Pit: An Amusement Mile fight club behind the arcade, bare knuckles and bets in cash; GCPD knows and gets paid not to.
notes.The Rookery: A Bowery club in a crumbling theatre, rooks painted on the ceiling and the Penguin's people at the bar.
notes.The Stacked Deck: A Diamond District card club for high rollers; the house always wins, and the house is Cobblepot.
notes.Velvet Hour: A Bowery cocktail lounge, red velvet and candlelight — the place to meet someone you shouldn't.
notes.Big Belly Burger: Gotham's favourite burger chain, Burnside branch: the Belly Buster, the shakes, and a queue at 2 a.m. that's half masked vigilantes, rumour says.
notes.Dixon's: A University District diner with a professor-for-a-day board and pancakes the size of the textbooks.
notes.Harbor Grill: An Old Gotham seafood diner where the clam chowder's been on the stove, in one form or another, since 1952.
notes.Jackie's: Burnley's all-day diner, run by Jackie for forty years; she knows your order and your business.
notes.Lucky Seven: A Tricorner diner open seven days and seven nights, lucky for anyone who needs eggs at 4 a.m. after a shift on the docks.
notes.Ma Gunn's: An Upper West Side diner with a reform-school past — Ma Gunn ran a school for young crooks once, and still cuts pie like a threat.
notes.Nite Owl: A Kane Heights night diner with an owl clock whose eyes follow you, and the best grilled cheese after midnight.
notes.Pearl's: A City Hall District lunch counter where aldermen eat meatloaf and make deals over rice pudding.
notes.Rosie's: A Coventry family diner with a rotating pie case and Rosie's grandchildren doing homework in the back booth.
notes.Sal's All-Night: Blüdhaven's Halyard Square diner, open all night every night; Dick has a booth and Sal has stopped asking about the bruises.
notes.The Blue Plate: A Crime Alley diner with a blue-plate special that hasn't changed since the Waynes were alive.
notes.The Midnight Diner: A Chinatown diner that only opens at midnight, cooking whatever you ask for if the chef has the ingredients.
notes.Engine 23: Burnside's firehouse, an old brick station with a dalmatian named Spot and a chili cook-off they always lose.
notes.Engine 41: Old Gotham's busiest firehouse; the old quarter's timber and tenements keep Engine 41 out every night.
notes.Engine 9: New Town's shiny firehouse, glass bay doors and a ladder truck that can reach the forty-second floor.
notes.Ladder 17: Robinsville's ladder company, famous for the night they saved a whole tenement and the mayor forgot to thank them.
notes.Ladder 4: The Upper West Side's ladder company, crews who know every brownstone fire escape by heart.
notes.Crossfire: A New Town CrossFit box where finance bros flip tractor tyres at six in the morning and talk about it all day.
notes.Iron Works Gym: A CBD power gym in an old foundry — chalk dust, iron plates, and a sign that says no mirrors, no excuses.
notes.Knuckle House: A Fashion District boxing studio for people who look good doing it; the owner was a contender once.
notes.Peak Fitness: The Upper East Side's members-only gym: steam rooms, personal trainers and memberships that cost a car.
notes.Southpaw Boxing: A Burnside boxing gym with a free youth programme — Jason's been seen in the back, teaching kids to keep their guard up.
notes.Wildcat Gym: Tricorner's old boxing gym, founded by the heavyweight Ted Grant; still sweat-soaked and still free for kids off the street.
notes.Harbor Inn: An Upper East Side hotel on the river, where visiting politicians stay to be seen being frugal.
notes.Hotel Noir: A Diamond District boutique hotel, all black marble and discretion; the night manager keeps secrets for a living.
notes.Hotel Ventura: An Old Gotham business hotel with a sky bar on the thirtieth floor and a view of Wayne Tower.
notes.Night & Day Motel: A CBD motel rented by the hour as often as the night; the sign flickers and so do the guests.
notes.The Ashcroft: The Fashion District's glass-tower hotel, rooftop pool and all, where new money comes to prove it.
notes.The Belvedere: A New Town art-deco hotel whose ballroom hosts the charity galas Bruce Wayne arrives late to.
notes.The Excelsior: The City Hall District's grand hotel, chandeliers and a doorman in livery; Gotham's old families have wedded here for a century.
notes.The Regency: The Diamond District's five-star hotel, presidential suites and a lobby where everybody knows whose money is whose.
notes.Cherry Hills Prep: A private school in Cherry Hills with a lacrosse obsession and a waiting list from birth.
notes.Gotham Heights High: An Upper West Side public high school with a good debate team and a terrible roof.
notes.PS 117: Bristol's public elementary, small and leafy, with Wayne Foundation computers and a gardening club.
notes.Robinson High: Coventry's high school, named for the park, with a football team that hasn't won since 1987.
notes.St. Mary's School: A Kane Heights Catholic school with plaid uniforms and nuns who've seen everything.
notes.Bluebird Boutique: A Chinatown boutique for one-off pieces, where Selina browses and the security guard pretends not to notice.
notes.Ellison's Jewelers: The Fashion District's oldest jeweller, robbed eleven times; the twelfth robber is, by tradition, Catwoman.
notes.Gotham Books: The Fashion District's big bookshop, four floors and a café; Tim's got a tab in true crime.
notes.Hart & Sons Tailors: A Fashion District tailor three generations deep; they've let out suits for men with very unusual shoulders and asked nothing.
notes.Madame Lacroix: An Old Gotham couture house where Gotham's society women order gowns a year before the gala.
notes.Rook & Pawn: A Diamond District pawnshop and chess hall; stolen goods move through the back, chess games through the front.
notes.Second Story Books: An Upper East Side used bookshop up a narrow staircase, its name a cat burglar's joke the owner swears is innocent.
notes.The Record Room: A Burnside record shop, crates of vinyl and listening booths; Dick sends Bruce photos of jazz records he'll never play.
notes.Vintage Vault: A Burnside vintage shop in an old bank, clothes racks in the vault and a cash register that was there for the last robbery.
notes.Engine 7: The Burnley firehouse, a red door in a brick row: they know every walk-up in the district by its fire escapes.
notes.Ladder 21: Crime Alley's ladder company, the busiest after Engine 33: the crews sleep in their boots.
notes.Engine 14: Chinatown's engine company under the expressway, its bay doors painted with a dragon the kids touch for luck.
notes.Engine 58: Coventry's firehouse by the market hall: Sunday chili for the neighbourhood, a dalmatian named Captain.
notes.Ladder 9: The Tricorner ladder company, among the dockworkers' rowhouses; half the crew grew up on the same street.
notes.Engine 30: Cherry Hills' engine company at the top of the hill, a brass pole from 1911 still in use.
notes.PS 41: Crime Alley's grade school behind a chain-link yard, the only building on the block without bars on the windows.
notes.Burnside Middle School: A five-storey brick school in Burnside with a rooftop yard and a waiting list for its after-school boxing club.
notes.Narrows Elementary: A school where morning announcements go out in three languages and the lunch line spills into the courtyard.
notes.New Town High: New Town's high school: its football team practises on a lot under the expressway ramps.
notes.Tricorner Community School: A school in a converted warehouse by the docks, run on donations and stubbornness.
notes.Park Row Academy of the Arts: An arts high school in an old textile mill off Park Row: practice rooms in the boiler house, murals on every wall, a guard on every door.
notes.Burnley High: Burnley's high school, a mid-century block of glass and terrazzo by the bus depot, its trophy case older than its teachers.
notes.GCPD 2nd Precinct: Burnley's station house, which works the corners the Burnley Town Massive runs and is outnumbered on every one of them.
notes.GCPD 5th Precinct: The Park Row precinct, the busiest desk in Gotham: its holding cells are full every night, and some of its officers are on someone's payroll.
notes.GCPD 8th Precinct: Chinatown's precinct, where a desk sergeant who speaks Cantonese and Fujianese is worth any three detectives.
notes.GCPD 9th Precinct: Coventry's station house by the river, quiet enough that its officers get loaned to everyone else's emergencies.
notes.GCPD 14th Precinct: The Upper West Side precinct in a limestone station house: burglaries, noise complaints, and the occasional body on the esplanade.
notes.GCPD 17th Precinct: New Town's precinct, which spends its nights at the bus terminal.
notes.GCPD 21st Precinct: Burnside's precinct, mostly bike thefts and bar fights, with a cyber unit nobody else in the GCPD has.
notes.GCPD 24th Precinct: The East End precinct by the freight yards: docks, warehouses, and cargo that falls off trucks.
notes.Tricorner Branch Library: A Carnegie library in Tricorner, the warmest room in the district all winter and the only quiet one.
notes.Coventry Library: Coventry's branch library on the circle, with a children's room upstairs and a chess club that has met every Tuesday since 1962.
notes.Burnley Library: A small branch above a bank, with newspapers in four languages and a librarian who has read everything.
notes.Burnside Public Library: Burnside's library in a glass box beside a mill, with a maker space, a podcast booth and late hours.
notes.Chinatown Library: Chinatown's branch: newspapers in three scripts, and a reading room where night-shift workers sleep in the armchairs and nobody wakes them.
notes.Corrigan's Market: Burnley's supermarket: a long fluorescent hall, a deli counter, and a security guard who has seen everything.
notes.Hollis Foods: Coventry's grocery on the high street: fruit stacked on the pavement, a butcher in the back.
notes.Greenway Grocers: A cramped Bowery grocery open till two, with dented cans and a cat asleep on the rice sacks.
notes.Delancey Foods: The Tricorner supermarket where the dockworkers buy their lunch and the night shift buys its breakfast.
notes.City Fresh: An Upper West Side grocer with a wine aisle, an olive bar and prices to match.
notes.Bodner's Supermarket: New Town's supermarket beside the bus terminal, open all night for the people waiting on late buses.
notes.Harbor Foods: Robinsville's market by the Coast Line halt: fresh fish off the boats and bait in the back.
notes.Kovac Bros. Grocery: A family grocery in Burnside for sixty years, now with a kombucha fridge the brothers pretend not to understand.
notes.Good Neighbor Market: The only grocery on the Narrows: one aisle, high prices, and credit for the regulars.
notes.Valu-Mart: Cherry Hills' discount supermarket at the bottom of the hill, its car park a meeting place after dark.
notes.Doane's Drugs: A Crime Alley pharmacy behind a steel shutter: methadone at the counter, a bulletproof window at the till.
notes.Gotham Rx: Burnley's chain pharmacy, open twenty-four hours; its night pharmacist knows half the district by its prescriptions.
notes.Mercy Pharmacy: A Chinatown pharmacy with Western medicine at the front and herbal remedies in the back drawers.
notes.Kessler's Chemist: An old-fashioned Upper West Side chemist: brass scales, apothecary jars, and house calls for the regulars.
notes.Night Owl Pharmacy: The Fashion District's all-night pharmacy, where models, nurses and cab drivers queue together at four in the morning.
notes.Lindqvist Drugs: The University District pharmacy, which does a roaring trade in coffee, cold remedies and exam-week vitamins.
notes.Corner Rx: Burnside's pharmacy with a soda fountain the new owners restored.
notes.Apothecary 1902: A Coventry pharmacy in the same tiled shop since 1902, run by the founder's great-granddaughter.
notes.Pyramid Gas: An Ironworks gas station on the truck route, lit like a stage all night.
notes.Kane Fuel: A gas station and diesel stop by the expressway ramps where the Ironworks shifts change.
notes.Harbor Gas & Go: The Robinsville gas station by the bridge ramps: fuel, coffee, and lottery tickets for the fishermen.
notes.24/7 Fuel Stop: New Town's all-night gas station, its forecourt where the cab drivers take their breaks.
notes.Comet Gas: A Kane Heights station with an old neon comet on its sign, as old as the heights' money.
notes.Burnside Service Station: A full-service station gone vintage: an attendant still checks your oil, and half the customers are fixing up old cars for the look.
notes.New Town Gas & Go: A gas station under the expressway ramps: a diner counter, showers for the drivers, and a car park where deals get done in cabs.
notes.First Gotham Savings: A Diamond District bank under a gilded ceiling, its vault famous enough to have been robbed in two films.
notes.Cobblepot Trust: An old private bank whose founding family lost it, and whose last heir wants it back.
notes.Gotham Federal Credit Union: The city workers' credit union, a plain glass branch in the Diamond District where GCPD pensions are paid.
notes.Mercantile Bank of Gotham: An Upper East Side bank for old money: no queue, no sign, a doorman.
notes.New Town Savings Bank: New Town's old savings bank under its clock, now half bank, half co-working space.
notes.Union Trust: New Town's mid-century bank tower, its night depository the busiest thing on the block after dark.
notes.Suds City: A Narrows laundromat that never closes, its dryers the warmest place on the island at three in the morning.
notes.Spin Cycle: A Bowery laundromat where the regulars mind each other's machines and the change machine is always broken.
notes.Clean Getaway: Burnley's laundromat, whose owner hears everything and repeats none of it.
notes.Wash & Fold 24: A Chinatown laundry with service by the pound, folded into neat squares by grandmothers who never miss a sock.
notes.Bubbles Laundromat: Robinsville's laundromat by the halt, smelling of soap and the sea.
notes.Lucky's Bodega: A Crime Alley bodega with bulletproof glass, a cat, and the best egg sandwich in the East End.
notes.Quick Stop: A Narrows corner store selling milk, batteries and burner phones, no questions asked.
notes.Ramirez Deli & Grocery: A Burnley bodega with a deli counter where the whole block gets its coffee.
notes.24 Hour Mini Mart: A Bowery mini-mart that has never closed, not even during No Man's Land.
notes.Corner Deli: Robinsville's corner shop, where the fishermen buy their cigarettes before dawn.
notes.Sunrise Bodega: The Tricorner bodega by the docks, open for the night shift's breakfast.
notes.Gotham Center Mall: New Town's indoor mall, three levels round a food court and an ice rink nobody has skated on since the 1990s.
notes.Otisburg Galleria: A glass mall at the foot of the Otisburg towers: flagship stores, a cinema, and a security team that never sleeps.
notes.Harbor Point Mall: Blüdhaven's waterfront mall, half its units empty and the rest selling to cruise passengers.
notes.The Lyceum: A Theater District house from 1903, gilt boxes and red plush, where the long-running musicals go.
notes.The Palace Theatre: The grandest stage in the Theater District, with first nights in black tie and a ghost the ushers won't talk about.
notes.The Orpheum: A Fashion District playhouse in a former vaudeville hall: experimental plays and revivals nobody expected to sell out.
notes.Old Gotham Post Office: A colonnaded post office in Old Gotham, its murals of the city's founding painted under the WPA.
notes.Burnside Post Office: Burnside's post office in a converted bank, its counters crowded with parcels from online shops.
notes.Burnley Post Office: Burnley's post office in an old bank, its counters crowded with parcels and a line out the door on the first of the month.
notes.Tilt: An Amusement Mile club in a shuttered pinball arcade: the machines still lit along the walls, a floor on a slope nobody ever fixed, and the DJ in the old change booth.
notes.Hall of Mirrors: A club in the Mile's old funhouse: a maze of mirrors to get in, a dance floor where you can't tell how many of anyone there are, and bouncers who like it that way.
notes.Last Ride: A New Town club in a disused tram depot: two old carriages for the booths, the rails painted gold, and last call at the hour the first car used to leave.
notes.Spin City Records: An Otisburg record shop of crates and listening booths, open till midnight, where the owner can find any pressing ever made and won't sell you half of them.
notes.Café Margaux: An Upper East Side café of marble tables and silver pots, where the nannies and the heiresses take the same window seats every morning.
notes.St. Bartholomew's: Upper East Side limestone and stained glass: society weddings on Saturdays, and a rector who knows every family's secrets.
notes.Hawthorne Academy: The Upper East Side's private school behind wrought-iron gates: blazers, Latin, and a waiting list from birth.
notes.Astor Library: A marble reading room on the Upper East Side, endowed by old money and kept hushed by librarians who've outlasted three mayors.
notes.Whitcombe Apothecary: An Upper East Side chemist with brass scales in the window, compounding by hand for clients who never wait in line.
notes.Maison Verrier: An Upper East Side jeweller by appointment only; the doorman decides who gets an appointment.
notes.Ashford & Lane: An Upper East Side department store of revolving doors and white-gloved lift operators, its windows the talk of the season.
notes.GCPD 19th Precinct: The Upper East Side's precinct house, polished brass and quiet complaints; its officers know which doors not to knock on.
notes.Delacroix Market: An Upper East Side gourmet grocer: truffles under glass, a cheese room, and delivery boys in bow ties.
notes.The Owl's Rest: An Upper West Side bar of bookshelves and low lamps, where professors argue over whisky till closing.
notes.Brownstone Coffee: An Upper West Side café on a brownstone's parlour floor: writers on laptops, a dog under every table.
notes.Westside Branch Library: The Upper West Side's busy branch library: story hour downstairs, chess players upstairs, and a line for the computers.
notes.Riverside Chapel: A stone chapel above the river on the Upper West Side: a soup kitchen on Tuesdays, organ concerts on Sundays.
notes.Folio & Spine: An Upper West Side bookshop of creaking floors and first editions, with a cat that sleeps in the poetry section.
notes.The Rialto: An Upper West Side revival house: old films on a single screen, real butter, and a projectionist who's never missed a reel.
notes.Mel's Family Diner: Robinsville's family diner: pancakes the size of hubcaps, booths full after Little League, and a waitress who calls everyone 'hon'.
notes.Robinsville Elementary: Robinsville's elementary school: a crossing guard named Gus, a playground with a rocket ship, and a bake sale every other Friday.
notes.Robinsville Library: A low brick library in Robinsville with a children's corner, tax help in spring, and the town's only free Wi-Fi.
notes.St. Brendan's: Robinsville's parish church: bingo on Wednesdays, a youth hall, and a priest who coaches the basketball team.
notes.Robinsville Pharmacy: A family pharmacy in a Robinsville strip mall, where the pharmacist knows every kid's allergies by name.
notes.The Daily Bread: A Robinsville bakery-café: warm rolls at six, parents after the school run, and gossip by the half-dozen.
notes.Champions Karate: A Robinsville karate dojo over a dry cleaner's: kids' classes after school, adults at night, and a sensei who takes no excuses.
notes.GCPD 26th Precinct: Robinsville's precinct house, mostly noise complaints and stolen bikes, until it isn't.
notes.The Summit: A Kane Heights bar at the top of a steep street; the view's worth the climb, the beer isn't.
notes.Hillside Coffee: A Kane Heights café with a terrace over the switchbacks, where cyclists recover and commuters refuel.
notes.Kane Heights Market: The neighbourhood grocer in Kane Heights: flowers out front, a deli counter, and credit for the regulars.
notes.Heights Pharmacy: A Kane Heights pharmacy open late, the only light on the hill after ten.
notes.Kane Heights Library: A small hilltop library in Kane Heights, endowed by the Kane family and named for one of them.
notes.Church of the Ascension: A Kane Heights church with a bell tower you can see from across the river.
notes.Hilltop Wash: A Kane Heights laundromat with a view of the whole city from its folding tables.
notes.The Greasy Spoon: A Narrows diner of cracked vinyl and coffee that never stops; nobody asks questions, and the cook keeps a bat under the counter.
notes.St. Dismas Mission: A Narrows mission church: cots in the basement, soup at noon, and a priest who's buried too many of his parishioners.
notes.Narrows Free Clinic Pharmacy: The free clinic's pharmacy in the Narrows: a line out the door by eight, bars on the windows, and a pharmacist who doesn't judge.
notes.Bricktown Boxing: A Narrows boxing gym in a converted garage, where kids learn to fight properly so they don't have to on the street.
notes.Lucky Seven Pawn: A Narrows pawn shop behind a wall of guitars; the owner asks nothing and remembers everything.
notes.Engine 66: The Narrows' firehouse, the busiest in Gotham, with a dalmatian named Sparky and a crew that's seen everything.
notes.GCPD 3rd Precinct: The Narrows' precinct house: bulletproof glass at the front desk and a holding cell that's never empty.
notes.The Orangery: A Bristol café in a glass orangery behind a garden centre: ladies who lunch, and the best scones in the county.
notes.Pemberton's Provisions: Bristol's old-fashioned grocer: wicker baskets, a butcher in a straw hat, and accounts settled monthly.
notes.Bristol Chemist: A quiet Bristol chemist's with a bell over the door and a pharmacist who delivers to the big houses.
notes.Bristol Trust Company: A Bristol private bank in a Georgian house, where the old families keep the money nobody talks about.
notes.The Bristol Arms: A coaching inn turned country hotel in Bristol: low beams, a fire in the bar, and rooms booked by people who don't want to be found.
notes.Hargreaves Antiques: A Bristol antiques shop of grandfather clocks and estate-sale silver, some of it with stories the owner won't tell.
notes.Bristol Free Library: A Bristol library in a former carriage house, with a reading garden and a local-history room nobody's catalogued.
notes.GCPD 30th Precinct: Bristol's sleepy precinct house: burglar alarms at the big houses and lost dogs, mostly.
notes.The Vineyard: A Cherry Hills wine bar of reclaimed oak and small plates, with quiet affairs in the corner booths.
notes.Cherry Hills Pharmacy: A bright Cherry Hills pharmacy with an espresso bar, as if medicine were a lifestyle.
notes.St. Catherine's: A white-steepled Cherry Hills church with a choir of very good voices and very competitive mothers.
notes.Hillcrest Savings: A Cherry Hills savings bank where the manager knows your father and your mortgage.
notes.Willow & Thread: A Cherry Hills boutique of linen, candles and gifts nobody needs, wrapped beautifully.
notes.Cherry Hills Racquet Club: A Cherry Hills tennis and fitness club with a waiting list, a clubhouse bar, and politics.
notes.Cherry Hills Post Office: A small post office in Cherry Hills with a flag out front and a clerk who reads every postcard.
notes.Byte Café: An Otisburg café full of laptops and hoodies, where startups are founded and folded over flat whites.
notes.Foundry Coffee: A roaster in an old Otisburg foundry: bare brick, single origins, and engineers arguing about code.
notes.The Server Room: An Otisburg bar with a terminal-green neon sign, craft beer on tap, and a trivia night the coders take very seriously.
notes.Gearbox Diner: An Otisburg diner from the factory days, still serving shift workers at dawn alongside the startup crowd.
notes.Circuit Fitness: A 24-hour Otisburg gym in a converted warehouse, its walls hung with the old factory's tools.
notes.Smokestack BBQ: An Otisburg barbecue joint under the old smokestack: brisket smoked overnight, and benches for the queue.
notes.The Otis: A design hotel in an Otisburg mill building: concrete, bare bulbs, and conference rooms booked by venture capitalists.
notes.The Scholar's Pint: The University District's student pub: pitchers, quiz night, and graffiti from a hundred graduating classes.
notes.Thesis: A University District cocktail bar for graduate students, named for what nobody's finished.
notes.Campus Books: The University District's bookstore: textbooks at robbery prices, a used section that's a treasure, and a café upstairs.
notes.The Varsity: An arthouse cinema in the University District: foreign films, and midnight cult screenings for the film society.
notes.Noodle Bar 88: Cheap noodles in the University District, open till three for students who forgot to eat.
notes.Varsity Athletic Club: The University District's student gym: rowing machines in rows, and the varsity crew at five in the morning.
notes.Spin & Study: A University District laundromat with Wi-Fi and study tables, where finals are crammed between the wash and the dry.
notes.University Post Office: A University District post office: care packages from home, and textbooks being sent back.
notes.The Coventry Arms: A Coventry corner pub with a dartboard, a jukebox, and the same six regulars since the eighties.
notes.Coventry Coin Wash: A Coventry laundromat run by a grandmother who folds your clothes whether you ask or not.
notes.Patel's Corner Store: A Coventry corner shop open every hour there is, its owner the neighbourhood's unofficial newsroom.
notes.Coventry Boxing Club: A Coventry boxing club above a hardware store: old fight posters on the walls and a coach who used to be somebody.
notes.Coventry Post Office: Coventry's post office: a queue on pension day and a clerk who knows everyone's business.
notes.Truck Stop 9: An Ironworks truck stop by the freight yards: steak and eggs at any hour, and drivers who've seen things on the night roads.
notes.The Rivet: An Ironworks bar for steelworkers: lunch-pail regulars and a union banner over the pool table.
notes.Anvil Gym: A bare-bones Ironworks gym of iron plates and chalk dust, where dockers and fighters train side by side.
notes.Ironworks Discount Foods: A warehouse grocer in the Ironworks: bulk everything, cash only, and a parking lot full of pickups.
notes.St. Joseph the Worker: An Ironworks church built by the steelworkers' union, its bell cast in the works itself.
notes.Engine 72: The Ironworks firehouse, trained for chemical fires and foundry accidents, and called out too often for both.
notes.The Coffee Cup: An Amusement Mile diner shaped like a giant coffee cup, still flipping burgers among the shuttered rides.
notes.The Carny: An Amusement Mile bar for the last of the carnival workers: sideshow posters, cheap whiskey, and a fortune teller in the back booth.
notes.Curios & Oddities: An Amusement Mile junk shop of old carousel horses, clown masks and fairground signs, run by a man who used to be a clown.
notes.Neon Moon Motel: A neon-signed motel on the Amusement Mile: rooms by the hour or the week, and nobody checking names.
